item.title: Re-escalating trade war puts Canada's economic rebound at risk: economists
item.description: Economists are warning that a re-escalation in the trade war with the United States puts Canada’s burgeoning economic recovery at risk.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Economists are warning that a re-escalation in the trade war with the United States puts Canada’s burgeoning economic recovery at risk. The U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after trade talks fell apart. The tariff targets, which include cement, honey, alcohol and textiles, amount to roughly five per cent of Canada’s exports to the United States. Bank of Montreal expects the new tariffs will carve half a percentage point off Canada’s economic growth as business investment and confidence take a hit. Before negotiations imploded on Friday, Canada’s economy had been showing signs of a rebound. Early reports from Statistics Canada have real gross domestic product on track for solid growth in the second quarter of 2026, coming off a pair of small contractions in the previous two quarters. “Unfortunately, this breakdown comes just as growth looked to be finding better momentum. Although businesses had been showing signs of looking past tariff headlines, this would be the toughest action since the spring of 2025,” said BMO senior economist Robert Kavcic in a note to clients over the weekend. Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged to retaliate with dollar-for-dollar tariffs starting Sept. 8. Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients Monday that the new tariffs push Canada closer to a recession, particularly if the United States ramps up attacks in response to Ottawa’s own retaliation. In a social media post Monday morning, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to impose steep 50 per cent tariffs on autos and parts starting Jan. 1, 2027. Economists say the extent of the overall hit to the economy will depend on the degree of fiscal stimulus from Canadian governments in response to the new U.S. duties. Saunders said he estimates Canada’s effective tariff rate — the average duty facing a Canadian good crossing the border — has now nearly doubled to 5.6 per cent from 2.9 per cent previously. Other economic shops had varying estimates of the new effective tariff rate on Monday, but most put it in the mid-to-high single digits. “Either way, the upshot is that Canada’s relative tariff advantage over other economies has taken a dent,” Saunders said. Both Saunders and Kavcic noted that there will likely be knock-on effects to the renegotiation of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico agreement, known as CUSMA. Businesses are now more likely to restrain investment decisions amid further uncertainty around the future of free trade in North America, they argued. Kavcic said the latest trade uncertainty is likely to reinforce the Bank of Canada’s decision to remain on hold. While counter-tariffs can stoke inflation, Kavcic argued those pressures would likely be offset by weaker growth in the trade war. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 24, 2026.

item.title: Loonie down in late-morning trading as U.S. imposes tariffs and Trump threatens more
item.description: The loonie fell against the U.S. dollar as the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods and threatened even more.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — The loonie fell against the U.S. dollar in late-morning trading as the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods and President Donald Trump threatened even more. The latest round of tariffs came after trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down on Friday night followed by fresh threats of tariff hikes on vehicles, auto parts and steel by Trump today.     The Canadian dollar traded for 72.27 cents US compared with 72.67 cents US on Friday.   “There are only mild market reactions thus far. CAD is the weakest performing major cross to the USD to start the week but is only about half-a-penny weaker since Friday’s close,” said Derek Holt, head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, in a note Monday morning.    He said weakness in the Canadian dollar was partially driven by lower oil prices and a “slightly firmer overall U.S. dollar.”    Sébastien Mc Mahon, chief economist at iA Financial Group, said in a statement that the loonie is one of the most shorted major currencies, “leaving much less room for further downside.”  The S&P/TSX composite index was down 15.03 points at 36,605.20.     Mc Mahon said the market reaction Monday is a signal that investors were not overly optimistic on the prospect of a U.S.-Canada trade deal.      He said technology stocks were providing some support for the TSX, while strength in gold prices was also helping.  The December gold contract was up US$51.40 at US$4,732.00 an ounce. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 157.59 points at 53,434.60. The S&P 500 index was down 11.76 points at 7,662.61, while the Nasdaq composite was down 95.70 points at 26,085.74. The October crude oil contract was down US$2.16 at US$84.90 per barrel. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 24, 2026.

item.title: ‘Their word is not their bond,’ policy expert slams last minute U.S. trade demands
item.description: Canada was right to impose counter-tariffs after the U.S. threatened its national sovereignty during trade talks, says a public policy expert.
item.dc:creator: Anam Khan
item.content:encoded: Canada was right to impose counter-tariffs after the U.S. threatened its national sovereignty during trade talks, says a public policy expert. The U.S. crossed the line by introducing issues that were “thrown in at the last minute,” which include higher tariffs for trucks, an attempt to restrict free trade deals with other nations, and an attempt to control content regulation in Canada, Drew Fagan, a professor at the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto, told BNN Bloomberg. “That’s extraordinarily sensitive,” he says. With the U.S. breaking its word even after Canada made painful concessions to secure a deal, Fagan says Prime Minister Mark Carney may feel “he has no choice but to introduce counter-tariffs.” Canada walked away from trade talks on Friday night after negotiations with the U.S. collapsed saying the U.S. “asked too much and they offered too little.” A 50 per cent tariff is now active on roughly $28 billion worth of goods. Carney vowed “Canada will match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses.” On Monday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to further escalate the trade war by increasing tariffs on Canadian auto, car parts and steel by 50 per cent on Jan. 1, 2027. Fagan says he hopes the dispute freezes at the current level of tariffs and counter-tariffs instead of escalating into a tit-for-tat war because, ultimately, it is Canada that hurts the most. “Canada’s not a small economy. It’s a medium-sized economy. But up against a super heavyweight, frankly, both tariffs and counter tariffs hurt Canada more than they do the U.S.,” says Fagan. “Let’s hope that politically, the Trump administration is hurt by this.” ‘Signature was written in pencil’ meaning On Friday, Carney stated the Canadian government understood that the U.S. would put “a series of tariffs on its closest allies and use economic integration as a weapon. That its signature was written in pencil.” Fagan says after seeing the deals the U.S. struck with other countries, and watching new demands come in at the last minute when Canada thought it was close to a deal, it is becoming clear what Carney meant. “Their word is not their bond,” says Fagan. He says unlike Japan, South Korea and the U.K., which accepted U.S. terms, Canada’s economy is too deeply integrated with the U.S. to blindly accept a deal. “So we’re learning from others, in effect, and that’s what he meant by written in pencil. Also, the fact that there were new demands at the last second when we thought we were close to a deal, a painful deal, a very painful deal, on Tuesday,” says Fagan. He says the U.S. is even trying to push Canada to give up its independence in making trade deals with other countries, particularly China. “That also was a bright line,” says Fagan. ‘The fight is really with China’ On Sunday, Trump wrote “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!” on his Truth Social account. Fagan explains that much of Trump’s understanding about bilateral relations is false. “The comments that his officials have made with regard to the Canada-U.S. relationship are almost apologetic,” says Fagan. “They don’t have a rationale for why they engaged in this offensive on trade terms, purely trade terms, given the depth of Canada-U.S. relations.” He says “the fight is really with China,” because the rise of China in global trade hurts manufacturing workers in both the U.S. and Canada, but the U.S. went after Canada instead. “The Western world, you could argue, made a strategic mistake with regard to the integration of China into the World Trade Organization and global trading,” says Fagan. “We should be an ally with the U.S. with regard to the issues that are on the table, as opposed to what we’ve been turned into by the Trump administration, which is a competitor.”
